Alfred Marshall. A late nineteenth and early twentieth century British economist who took Adam Smith's vision of self-regulating markets and gave it mathematical precision.

Marshall showed how supply and demand interact in a single market, with price as the mechanism that makes them equal. He introduced the concept of elasticity, which measures how responsive the quantity people want to buy is to changes in price. A steep demand curve means people are not very responsive to price changes. A flat one means they are very responsive. He developed the theory of consumer surplus and producer surplus, giving economists a way to measure the welfare gains from trade.

Before Marshall, there was a gap between classical economics, which focused on land rent, and the newer utility theory, which focused on marginal satisfaction. Marshall bridged this divide. He showed how all factor prices—wages, profits, rents, interest—are determined by marginal productivity. That is, how much an additional unit of input contributes to total output.

Marshall believed economists needed to study industrial organization systematically. He wanted to understand how firms compete, merge, and grow. This work laid the foundations for later studies of monopoly, cartels, and antitrust economics.

Crucially, Marshall championed the use of mathematics and graphs in economics. He developed the Marshallian cross diagram, with supply and demand curves intersecting to show equilibrium price and quantity. This simple diagram became the language of economics, establishing the modern quantitative tradition that economists still use today. His textbook, Principles of Economics, published in 1890, became the standard for nearly fifty years and established Cambridge as the global center of economics. His student John Maynard Keynes later challenged Marshall's fundamental assumption that markets always reach equilibrium and full employment, but Marshall's framework remained at the heart of microeconomic analysis.
